parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 17. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a man phoning to find out about a children's holiday club that takes place in a wood. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 3. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 3. Karen: Good morning, Woodland Explorers. Karen speaking. Paul: Oh, hello. I saw a leaflet about your holiday club, and I'd like some more information, please. Karen: Of course. What would you like to know? Paul: Well, I've got two children. My son, Toby, is five. Is he old enough to come? Karen: Yes, he is. He'd be in our Little Explorers group, which is for children aged four to six. Paul: And what kind of things do they do? He's never really spent much time in the countryside. Karen: Oh, lots of things. On the first day, they work together to build a den, using fallen branches and leaves. It's big enough for them all to sit inside, and they absolutely love it. Paul: That sounds great. Toby's always making camps out of the cushions at home. Karen: Then they learn to recognise different trees and plants, and we test them on that with a treasure hunt. They have to find things like an oak leaf or a pine cone, and there's a small prize at the end. Paul: He'd enjoy that. Do they do any art or anything like that? Karen: Yes, but not with ordinary paints. We make paint by mixing mud with a little water, and the children use it to paint pictures on old pieces of wood. It's very messy, but that's part of the fun. Paul: I'll make sure he wears old clothes, then. Karen: That's a good idea. And don't worry about him being looked after. The groups are small, with no more than twelve children, and there are always three members of staff with each group. Paul: That's reassuring. He can be a bit shy with new people at first. Karen: Most of them are on the first morning, but they soon settle in once they're outside and busy. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 4 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 4 to 10. Paul: My daughter, Grace, is nine. Would she be in a different group? Karen: Yes, she'd join the Big Explorers. That's for children from seven to ten. Paul: And do they do the same sort of things? Karen: Some of it is similar, but it's a bit more challenging. For example, they learn how to light a fire safely, and how to put it out properly afterwards. There's always a member of staff right next to them, of course. Paul: And do they cook on it? Karen: They do. We used to let them toast marshmallows, but some parents weren't happy about all the sugar, so now they cook popcorn over the fire instead, in a special pan with a long handle. It's much more popular than you'd think. Paul: I'm sure. What else? Karen: Well, we hide objects around the wood, and they have to find them using a compass. We don't give them a map, just the compass and a set of directions, so they really have to concentrate. Paul: Grace is good at that sort of thing. She's in the Scouts. Karen: Then she'll do well. And on the last day, each child carves a spoon from a piece of wood. They use special knives, and they're very closely supervised. It takes most of the day, but they're really proud of what they make, and they get to take it home. Paul: That's a lovely idea. And when are the sessions? I'm working most days, so I need to plan ahead. Karen: We used to run them on Mondays and Wednesdays, but this summer they're on Tuesdays and Thursdays, from half past nine until three. Paul: OK, that should be fine. And how much does it cost? Karen: It's eighty-five pounds per child for the week. It went up this year, I'm afraid. It was seventy-five pounds last summer. But that does include all the materials. Paul: Is there any reduction if two children from the same family come? Karen: I'm afraid not. We've kept the price as low as we can, so it's the same for every child. Paul: OK, well, that's still reasonable. And where exactly do you meet? Is it the wood near the golf course? Karen: No, that's a different one. We're in Rodbrook Wood, just off the Oxford road. Paul: Sorry, could you spell that? Karen: Yes, it's R, O, D, B, R, O, O, K. There's a small car park at the entrance, and we meet by the wooden gate. Paul: Great. And do they need to bring anything? Karen: Just a packed lunch, a water bottle and a waterproof jacket. We go out whatever the weather. Paul: Fine. I'd like to book places for both of them, please. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a theatre welcoming a group of new volunteers. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Speaker: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the Riverside Playhouse. Thank you all for offering to give up some of your free time to help us. My name's Sarah Bennett, and I've been the manager here for the last six years. Before we look round, I thought I'd tell you a little about the history of the building, because visitors often ask about it, and it's useful for you to know. Speaker: The building itself is older than most people realise. It was put up in nineteen oh eight. But for its first twenty-five years or so, it wasn't a theatre at all. A local company bought it in nineteen twenty-nine with plans to convert it, but work was delayed by a shortage of money, and the Playhouse didn't actually open its doors as a theatre until nineteen thirty-four. Speaker: So what was it before that? Well, a lot of people assume it must have been a cinema, because it did show films for a few years in the nineteen fifties, when audiences for live theatre were falling. And there was once a plan to turn it into a concert hall, but that never happened. In fact, it was built as a covered market, where local farmers sold fruit, vegetables and cheese. If you look carefully at the front of the building, you can still see the word Market carved above the main entrance. Speaker: Now, you may have heard that we've got some changes coming up. We did look into making the stage larger, but it would have been far too expensive, and the number of seats will stay the same as well. What we are going to do, next spring, is open a café at the side of the building, so that people can come in during the day, not just for performances. Speaker: As for your first week with us, it'll be a mixture of things. In the past, new volunteers used to have a chance to meet some of the actors, but with the current production, that isn't possible, I'm afraid. However, you'll all be doing a first aid course on Saturday morning, which is required for everyone who works front of house. And you'll spend a couple of evenings shadowing one of our experienced volunteers. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Speaker: Right, now let me help you find your way around the ground floor. Have a look at the plan I've given you. We're standing just inside the main entrance, in the foyer. The room on your left as you come in is the box office, which I'm sure you noticed on your way in. And the door immediately on your right, as you come through the main entrance, leads into the volunteers' room. That's where you'll leave your coats and bags, and there's a kettle in there, too. Speaker: Now, at the back of the foyer, on the left, there's a corridor that runs along the side of the auditorium. If you go along that corridor, the first door on your left is the costume store. You won't often need to go in there, but you might be asked to fetch something for the wardrobe team. Speaker: On the other side of the auditorium, there's a matching corridor. So from the foyer, you go through the door at the back on the right, and the first door on your right is the green room. That's where the actors relax before they go on stage, so please knock before you go in. Speaker: Back in the left-hand corridor, if you walk past the costume store, the next door on your left takes you into the rehearsal studio. It's a big, bright room, and we sometimes use it for school workshops, so you may be helping out in there. Speaker: Then there's the bar. That's here in the foyer, on the right-hand side, just in front of the doors into the auditorium. On the opposite side of the foyer there's a desk where we sell programmes, and that's where most of you will be working on your first few evenings. Speaker: And finally, if you need to find me, my office is at the very end of the left-hand corridor. It's the last door on the left, in the corner of the building, just before you reach the passage that leads to the stage door. Speaker: OK, are there any questions before we go and have a look around? That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two museum studies students called Maya and Sam discussing their placement at the university museum. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Maya: Hi, Sam. How's the museum placement going? Sam: Not bad, thanks. I've more or less finished the introductory stage now. What about you? Maya: Same here. I have to admit, I wasn't looking forward to the training on the online catalogue. I thought it would be really dull. Sam: So did I, but it turned out to be really useful. Now I can find out almost anything about an object in a couple of minutes. Maya: Exactly. I use it all the time now. What did you think of the tour of the storerooms? Sam: Honestly, I found it a bit disappointing. We just walked past rows of boxes. We didn't actually see anything. Maya: Really? I thought it was fascinating, seeing how much is kept behind the scenes. Sam: Well, maybe. But the handling session was the best part for me, actually picking up objects and learning how to look after them. Maya: Oh, definitely. I learned more in that one morning than in the rest of the week. It's a shame the curator's talk was cancelled, though. Sam: Yes, and the visit to the city museum was postponed too, so we'll have to wait for that. Maya: So, have you written your exhibition proposal yet? Sam: I've done a first draft, but I showed it to our supervisor, and she said my labels were far too long. She said visitors only spend a few seconds reading each one, so I'll have to cut them down. Maya: Oh, mine are quite long as well. I'd better shorten them too. Did she say anything else? Sam: Yes, she said it wasn't enough just to describe the objects. We need to explain how each one came to be in the museum, who collected it and why. So I'm going to add a short section on that. Maya: That's a good point. I hadn't thought about that. I'll add something about that to mine. Sam: I was also thinking of including a digital display with photos, but the supervisor said there isn't a screen available, so I've dropped that. Maya: Oh, that's a pity. I'd been thinking of changing my title, too, but actually I think I'll keep it as it is. Sam: And what about the number of objects? Some people in our group have chosen ten or twelve. Maya: I asked her about that. She said six is plenty, so neither of us needs to add any more. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Sam: Now, the part I'm finding hardest is where we have to say what each object means to us personally. Shall we go through the ones we've chosen? Maya: Good idea. Well, my first one is the map of the town from eighteen sixty. I compared it with a modern map, and half the streets on it have completely disappeared. There was a river running through the middle of town that's now under a car park. Sam: So for you it's about how quickly places can change? Maya: Yes, exactly. What about you? You chose the ship's compass, didn't you? Sam: I did. At first I was going to write about the dangers sailors faced, but that's not really what it means to me. When I was deciding whether to come to university, everyone was giving me advice, and in the end I had to make up my own mind. So for me, the compass is about choosing your own direction and making your own decisions. Maya: That's nice. My next one is the wooden horse. It's a child's toy from around nineteen hundred. Sam: You could talk about the skill of the carving. It's beautifully made. Maya: I could, but actually the reason I chose it is that my grandfather made me one just like it when I was about four. I still remember him working on it in his shed, so it takes me straight back to being a little girl. Sam: Lovely. OK, then I've got the ice skates made of animal bone. Apparently people used them on frozen rivers hundreds of years ago. Maya: Are you going to say something about simple pleasures, having fun without spending money? Sam: I thought about it. But what really strikes me is that those winters were incredibly hard. People couldn't work, and food was running out, and yet they found a way to get through it. So for me, the skates are about how people cope with difficult times. Maya: That's a good angle. Then there's my Roman oil lamp. Sam: What does that mean to you? Maya: Well, it made me think about people reading and studying by lamplight. My mum was a teacher, and she always said the most important thing you can do is pass on what you know to other people. So I'm going to write about sharing knowledge. Sam: Great. And my last one is the old clock from the museum entrance. Maya: Why did you choose that? Sam: Because it's been ticking in the same place for over a hundred years, while generations of students have come and gone. It reminds me that time passes, whether we notice it or not. Maya: That's a bit sad, but I like it. I think we've got a good selection. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk on the ancient philosophy of Epicureanism. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: Today I'd like to talk about a philosophy that is often misunderstood, and that's Epicureanism. If you look up the word epicure in a modern dictionary, you'll find that it describes someone who enjoys expensive food and wine. So you might expect the founder of this philosophy to have lived a life of luxury. In fact, the opposite is true, and I hope that by the end of this talk you'll see why his ideas are still worth taking seriously. Lecturer: Epicurus was born on the Greek island of Samos in three forty-one BC. Around three oh seven BC, he moved to Athens and set up his own school. Unlike other philosophers of the time, who taught in public buildings or in the market place, Epicurus bought a house with a garden just outside the city, and his school met in that garden. In fact, his followers became known simply as the Garden. According to one ancient writer, a sign above the garden gate told visitors that here, the highest good was pleasure. Lecturer: The school was unusual in another way, too. Most philosophical schools in Athens were open only to free men. Epicurus, however, welcomed women and even slaves as members, which was quite shocking at the time. Lecturer: And what about that reputation for luxury? Well, life in the Garden was actually very simple. Epicurus and his followers lived mainly on bread and water, with a little wine on special occasions. In one of his letters that has survived, he asks a friend to send him a small pot of cheese, so that he can have a feast whenever he wants. That tells you a great deal about his idea of luxury. Lecturer: So what did Epicurus actually teach? He did believe that pleasure was the goal of life, and that's where the confusion comes from. But by pleasure he meant something quite different from what we might expect. For Epicurus, the greatest pleasure was simply the absence of pain in the body and freedom from anxiety in the mind. He argued that expensive meals and fame only create new desires, which leave us less satisfied than before. Lecturer: Of all the things that could make a person happy, Epicurus believed that the most important was friendship. He is said to have written that, of everything wisdom provides for a happy life, the greatest by far is the possession of friends. He also taught that people should not fear death. His argument was that when we exist, death is not present, and when death is present, we no longer exist, so there is nothing to be afraid of. Lecturer: Very little of what Epicurus wrote has survived. Most of what we know about his ideas comes from a long poem called On the Nature of Things, written by the Roman poet Lucretius in the first century BC. For centuries, this poem was thought to be lost. Then, in fourteen seventeen, an Italian book collector found a copy in a monastery in Germany, and his discovery helped to spread Epicurean ideas across Renaissance Europe. Lecturer: The poem is remarkable for its scientific ideas. Following earlier Greek thinkers, Epicurus believed that everything in the universe, including the human body and mind, was made up of tiny particles called atoms, moving through empty space. He also argued that the gods, if they existed, took no interest in human affairs. Many of his later readers found these ideas deeply shocking, and for a long time Epicureans were regarded with great suspicion. Lecturer: Since then, Epicurus has influenced many important thinkers. The American president Thomas Jefferson once described himself in a letter as an Epicurean. And the young Karl Marx chose to write his doctoral thesis on the differences between the ideas of Epicurus and those of an earlier Greek philosopher, Democritus. Lecturer: Today, interestingly, modern research seems to support some of Epicurus's ideas. Studies of happiness have found that once people have enough money to meet their basic needs, earning more makes surprisingly little difference to how satisfied they are with their lives. What matters far more is having strong relationships with other people. Epicurus would not have been surprised. Lecturer: Of course, living as an Epicurean is not as easy as it sounds. It means questioning many of the things our society tells us we should want. But the basic message, that a good life depends on friends, simple pleasures and a calm mind, seems as relevant now as it was over two thousand years ago. That is the end of Part 4. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a theatre welcoming a group of new volunteers. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Speaker: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the Riverside Playhouse. Thank you all for offering to give up some of your free time to help us. My name's Sarah Bennett, and I've been the manager here for the last six years. Before we look round, I thought I'd tell you a little about the history of the building, because visitors often ask about it, and it's useful for you to know. Speaker: The building itself is older than most people realise. It was put up in nineteen oh eight. But for its first twenty-five years or so, it wasn't a theatre at all. A local company bought it in nineteen twenty-nine with plans to convert it, but work was delayed by a shortage of money, and the Playhouse didn't actually open its doors as a theatre until nineteen thirty-four. Speaker: So what was it before that? Well, a lot of people assume it must have been a cinema, because it did show films for a few years in the nineteen fifties, when audiences for live theatre were falling. And there was once a plan to turn it into a concert hall, but that never happened. In fact, it was built as a covered market, where local farmers sold fruit, vegetables and cheese. If you look carefully at the front of the building, you can still see the word Market carved above the main entrance. Speaker: Now, you may have heard that we've got some changes coming up. We did look into making the stage larger, but it would have been far too expensive, and the number of seats will stay the same as well. What we are going to do, next spring, is open a café at the side of the building, so that people can come in during the day, not just for performances. Speaker: As for your first week with us, it'll be a mixture of things. In the past, new volunteers used to have a chance to meet some of the actors, but with the current production, that isn't possible, I'm afraid. However, you'll all be doing a first aid course on Saturday morning, which is required for everyone who works front of house. And you'll spend a couple of evenings shadowing one of our experienced volunteers. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Speaker: Right, now let me help you find your way around the ground floor. Have a look at the plan I've given you. We're standing just inside the main entrance, in the foyer. The room on your left as you come in is the box office, which I'm sure you noticed on your way in. And the door immediately on your right, as you come through the main entrance, leads into the volunteers' room. That's where you'll leave your coats and bags, and there's a kettle in there, too. Speaker: Now, at the back of the foyer, on the left, there's a corridor that runs along the side of the auditorium. If you go along that corridor, the first door on your left is the costume store. You won't often need to go in there, but you might be asked to fetch something for the wardrobe team. Speaker: On the other side of the auditorium, there's a matching corridor. So from the foyer, you go through the door at the back on the right, and the first door on your right is the green room. That's where the actors relax before they go on stage, so please knock before you go in. Speaker: Back in the left-hand corridor, if you walk past the costume store, the next door on your left takes you into the rehearsal studio. It's a big, bright room, and we sometimes use it for school workshops, so you may be helping out in there. Speaker: Then there's the bar. That's here in the foyer, on the right-hand side, just in front of the doors into the auditorium. On the opposite side of the foyer there's a desk where we sell programmes, and that's where most of you will be working on your first few evenings. Speaker: And finally, if you need to find me, my office is at the very end of the left-hand corridor. It's the last door on the left, in the corner of the building, just before you reach the passage that leads to the stage door. Speaker: OK, are there any questions before we go and have a look around? That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two museum studies students called Maya and Sam discussing their placement at the university museum. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Maya: Hi, Sam. How's the museum placement going? Sam: Not bad, thanks. I've more or less finished the introductory stage now. What about you? Maya: Same here. I have to admit, I wasn't looking forward to the training on the online catalogue. I thought it would be really dull. Sam: So did I, but it turned out to be really useful. Now I can find out almost anything about an object in a couple of minutes. Maya: Exactly. I use it all the time now. What did you think of the tour of the storerooms? Sam: Honestly, I found it a bit disappointing. We just walked past rows of boxes. We didn't actually see anything. Maya: Really? I thought it was fascinating, seeing how much is kept behind the scenes. Sam: Well, maybe. But the handling session was the best part for me, actually picking up objects and learning how to look after them. Maya: Oh, definitely. I learned more in that one morning than in the rest of the week. It's a shame the curator's talk was cancelled, though. Sam: Yes, and the visit to the city museum was postponed too, so we'll have to wait for that. Maya: So, have you written your exhibition proposal yet? Sam: I've done a first draft, but I showed it to our supervisor, and she said my labels were far too long. She said visitors only spend a few seconds reading each one, so I'll have to cut them down. Maya: Oh, mine are quite long as well. I'd better shorten them too. Did she say anything else? Sam: Yes, she said it wasn't enough just to describe the objects. We need to explain how each one came to be in the museum, who collected it and why. So I'm going to add a short section on that. Maya: That's a good point. I hadn't thought about that. I'll add something about that to mine. Sam: I was also thinking of including a digital display with photos, but the supervisor said there isn't a screen available, so I've dropped that. Maya: Oh, that's a pity. I'd been thinking of changing my title, too, but actually I think I'll keep it as it is. Sam: And what about the number of objects? Some people in our group have chosen ten or twelve. Maya: I asked her about that. She said six is plenty, so neither of us needs to add any more. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Sam: Now, the part I'm finding hardest is where we have to say what each object means to us personally. Shall we go through the ones we've chosen? Maya: Good idea. Well, my first one is the map of the town from eighteen sixty. I compared it with a modern map, and half the streets on it have completely disappeared. There was a river running through the middle of town that's now under a car park. Sam: So for you it's about how quickly places can change? Maya: Yes, exactly. What about you? You chose the ship's compass, didn't you? Sam: I did. At first I was going to write about the dangers sailors faced, but that's not really what it means to me. When I was deciding whether to come to university, everyone was giving me advice, and in the end I had to make up my own mind. So for me, the compass is about choosing your own direction and making your own decisions. Maya: That's nice. My next one is the wooden horse. It's a child's toy from around nineteen hundred. Sam: You could talk about the skill of the carving. It's beautifully made. Maya: I could, but actually the reason I chose it is that my grandfather made me one just like it when I was about four. I still remember him working on it in his shed, so it takes me straight back to being a little girl. Sam: Lovely. OK, then I've got the ice skates made of animal bone. Apparently people used them on frozen rivers hundreds of years ago. Maya: Are you going to say something about simple pleasures, having fun without spending money? Sam: I thought about it. But what really strikes me is that those winters were incredibly hard. People couldn't work, and food was running out, and yet they found a way to get through it. So for me, the skates are about how people cope with difficult times. Maya: That's a good angle. Then there's my Roman oil lamp. Sam: What does that mean to you? Maya: Well, it made me think about people reading and studying by lamplight. My mum was a teacher, and she always said the most important thing you can do is pass on what you know to other people. So I'm going to write about sharing knowledge. Sam: Great. And my last one is the old clock from the museum entrance. Maya: Why did you choose that? Sam: Because it's been ticking in the same place for over a hundred years, while generations of students have come and gone. It reminds me that time passes, whether we notice it or not. Maya: That's a bit sad, but I like it. I think we've got a good selection. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk on the ancient philosophy of Epicureanism. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: Today I'd like to talk about a philosophy that is often misunderstood, and that's Epicureanism. If you look up the word epicure in a modern dictionary, you'll find that it describes someone who enjoys expensive food and wine. So you might expect the founder of this philosophy to have lived a life of luxury. In fact, the opposite is true, and I hope that by the end of this talk you'll see why his ideas are still worth taking seriously. Lecturer: Epicurus was born on the Greek island of Samos in three forty-one BC. Around three oh seven BC, he moved to Athens and set up his own school. Unlike other philosophers of the time, who taught in public buildings or in the market place, Epicurus bought a house with a garden just outside the city, and his school met in that garden. In fact, his followers became known simply as the Garden. According to one ancient writer, a sign above the garden gate told visitors that here, the highest good was pleasure. Lecturer: The school was unusual in another way, too. Most philosophical schools in Athens were open only to free men. Epicurus, however, welcomed women and even slaves as members, which was quite shocking at the time. Lecturer: And what about that reputation for luxury? Well, life in the Garden was actually very simple. Epicurus and his followers lived mainly on bread and water, with a little wine on special occasions. In one of his letters that has survived, he asks a friend to send him a small pot of cheese, so that he can have a feast whenever he wants. That tells you a great deal about his idea of luxury. Lecturer: So what did Epicurus actually teach? He did believe that pleasure was the goal of life, and that's where the confusion comes from. But by pleasure he meant something quite different from what we might expect. For Epicurus, the greatest pleasure was simply the absence of pain in the body and freedom from anxiety in the mind. He argued that expensive meals and fame only create new desires, which leave us less satisfied than before. Lecturer: Of all the things that could make a person happy, Epicurus believed that the most important was friendship. He is said to have written that, of everything wisdom provides for a happy life, the greatest by far is the possession of friends. He also taught that people should not fear death. His argument was that when we exist, death is not present, and when death is present, we no longer exist, so there is nothing to be afraid of. Lecturer: Very little of what Epicurus wrote has survived. Most of what we know about his ideas comes from a long poem called On the Nature of Things, written by the Roman poet Lucretius in the first century BC. For centuries, this poem was thought to be lost. Then, in fourteen seventeen, an Italian book collector found a copy in a monastery in Germany, and his discovery helped to spread Epicurean ideas across Renaissance Europe. Lecturer: The poem is remarkable for its scientific ideas. Following earlier Greek thinkers, Epicurus believed that everything in the universe, including the human body and mind, was made up of tiny particles called atoms, moving through empty space. He also argued that the gods, if they existed, took no interest in human affairs. Many of his later readers found these ideas deeply shocking, and for a long time Epicureans were regarded with great suspicion. Lecturer: Since then, Epicurus has influenced many important thinkers. The American president Thomas Jefferson once described himself in a letter as an Epicurean. And the young Karl Marx chose to write his doctoral thesis on the differences between the ideas of Epicurus and those of an earlier Greek philosopher, Democritus. Lecturer: Today, interestingly, modern research seems to support some of Epicurus's ideas. Studies of happiness have found that once people have enough money to meet their basic needs, earning more makes surprisingly little difference to how satisfied they are with their lives. What matters far more is having strong relationships with other people. Epicurus would not have been surprised. Lecturer: Of course, living as an Epicurean is not as easy as it sounds. It means questioning many of the things our society tells us we should want. But the basic message, that a good life depends on friends, simple pleasures and a calm mind, seems as relevant now as it was over two thousand years ago. That is the end of Part 4. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
